title: Moving to a Better Neighborhood
text:
In the mid-1990s, the United States government ran an experiment called Moving to Opportunity. In five cities, Baltimore, Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles and New York, families living in high-poverty public housing could sign up for a lottery. Some were offered vouchers to help pay rent, on condition that they move to a low-poverty neighborhood. Others received ordinary vouchers or nothing extra. Because the offers were random, the families could be fairly compared.

Earlier studies found that the moves improved adults' mental and physical health in some ways but did little for their earnings, and many concluded that neighborhoods did not matter much economically.

In 2016, the economists Raj Chetty, Nathaniel Hendren and Lawrence Katz looked again, this time at the children, using tax records to follow them into adulthood. The age at which a child moved turned out to matter greatly. Children whose families had moved to a lower-poverty neighborhood before they turned thirteen went on to earn substantially more in their mid-twenties than children in the control group, were more likely to attend college and less likely to become single parents. For children who moved as teenagers, there was no such gain, and possibly some harm.

The benefits seemed to grow with every year a child spent in the better environment.
lesson: Where a child grows up shapes their future, and the years of childhood add up. Decisions about home and neighborhood are among the biggest a family makes.
people: Raj Chetty, Nathaniel Hendren, Lawrence Katz
location: Baltimore, Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles and New York, USA
source: Chetty, R., Hendren, N., and Katz, L. F. (2016). The effects of exposure to better neighborhoods on children: New evidence from the Moving to Opportunity experiment. American Economic Review, 106(4), 855-902.
